title: Gorman's melodic style and playing close to the tune
summary: Gorman describes staying close to the melody in small bands and his professor's advice about thirds and fifths.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well that's the idea. Sometime they'd cover, cover right, and they'd make the notes form, and sometime they'd half-cover, well it was a bad note, but you tell them anything, they'd say, man that note is bad. I said, no that note ain't bad, it's just a passing tone. You mean he was passing, you understand what I mean? And he didn't just pass at the right place, he passed in the wrong spot, you see. Well it's just a bad tone. But I always did believe in hitting something right, see. And when I fingered, I had to fingered it right. If I had to take me two hours just to get that one note, I'm gonna get it right. And when I started out, I'm gonna have it there. You see that's mostly my way of playing. Now I don't play a lot of that stuff that you see them fellas do on the client, that sometime you be playing so much, sometime you don't know if they're playing circus music, or you don't know if they're playing dance music. It's too much, I play just enough, but I don't stay, but I stay as to my melody, I don't get away from my melody no more than a third. That's the closest I get away from my melody. I'm always gonna let you know what I'm doing. But to play my clarinet and play a seven or a nine chord, I don't never get that far. The only way I get that far if I'm playing in the big band. And now that big band has got the root. If you've got the root, well then I can go on and get the ninth chord. I know how to get back, or seventh chord you see, because I have somebody holding my melody. See but if you're playing with a small band, you know Mr. Bill, like say, band, five piece band, man, seven and ninth chord's too far. You're modulating other keys when you're getting away. But a lot of the fellas they play it that way. When I play my instrument, something like this fella Louis Armstrong, I stay as close to my melody at all times. Nine and then I may get maybe a fifth. But I don't get too far from the fifth. I stay right from the root to the third. See, because I know right back to get back. And I'm going to always let you know I'm going to play playing it, see. If I be playing the Musrat Ramble I may go to the third. But every now and then when I think that you don't know what I'm doing I jump right back on the root and jump the lead. And I may play the lead me for but four balls to let you know I'm playing the Musrat Ramble and then I get back again. You see now that's my way of playing, you see. Well this professor would learn me to, he always would tell me that. He say, you mix yourself. He said you play with a small band, the four you get away from that band is a third. Now and then you go to fifth. But be sure to don't stay no, don't you go to no seventh. See don't ever get no foot at next. Now if you go to sixth, always make maybe a passing tone to try to get back to your melody as close as you can, you know what I mean? Because the people wants to know what you playing. See, because if you get too far off, sometimes you get confused and you don't know how to get back. That's why you mix the buzz out. That's why mostly I've been making pretty good in my planning. Like every place I ever worked at, I always was well-liked with the people. You know the man I work with. Sure. They always tell me that I really did my work right. I never tried to imitate no one else. I played on my own style. See, and I done worked in many places. I worked, you remember the time, I believe you brought a gentleman over there.
